Learning the policy directly

Most methods so far learned values and acted greedily (or ε-greedily) on them. Policy-gradient methods skip that step. The policy gets its own parameters $\boldsymbol\theta$, and learning means nudging $\boldsymbol\theta$ uphill on the return. In some problems the best policy is a weighted coin flip, which no greedy rule can express.

The short corridor with switched actions

S&B Example 13.1. Reward $-1$ per step until the flag. In the yellow state, the actions are swapped: right moves left and left moves right. The agent cannot tell the three states apart, so it must use the same action probabilities everywhere.

Drag the sliders, then run an episode.

Green curve: the exact value of the start state, $J$, for every probability of right $p$. Green dot: your policy. Grey dots: the two ε-greedy policies ($\varepsilon = 0.1$). Blue dot: the average return of your last 1000 episodes. "Climb" follows the slope of $J$ uphill by changing $\boldsymbol\theta$.

The maths

A parameterised policy gives the probability of each action from a parameter vector $\boldsymbol\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}$:

$$\pi(a \mid s, \boldsymbol\theta) = \Pr\{A_t = a \mid S_t = s, \boldsymbol\theta_t = \boldsymbol\theta\}$$

No value function is needed to pick actions. The usual choice for discrete actions is a softmax over action preferences $h(s, a, \boldsymbol\theta)$, as in Lesson 13:

$$\pi(a \mid s, \boldsymbol\theta) = \frac{e^{h(s,a,\boldsymbol\theta)}}{\sum_b e^{h(s,b,\boldsymbol\theta)}}, \qquad h(s,a,\boldsymbol\theta) = \boldsymbol\theta^\top \mathbf{x}(s,a)$$

The preference is linear in a feature vector $\mathbf{x}(s,a)$. In the corridor, $\mathbf{x}(s,\text{right}) = (1,0)^\top$ and $\mathbf{x}(s,\text{left}) = (0,1)^\top$ in every state, so

$$p = \pi(\text{right}) = \frac{e^{\theta_1}}{e^{\theta_1} + e^{\theta_2}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\theta_1 - \theta_2)}}$$

Only the difference $\theta_1 - \theta_2$ matters.

The performance measure for an episodic task is the value of the start state, and learning is gradient ascent on it:

$$J(\boldsymbol\theta) = v_{\pi_{\boldsymbol\theta}}(s_0), \qquad \boldsymbol\theta_{t+1} = \boldsymbol\theta_t + \alpha\, \widehat{\nabla J(\boldsymbol\theta_t)}$$

$\widehat{\nabla J}$ is an estimate of the gradient. Lessons 71 to 73 show how to get one from experience alone.

The corridor's $J$ by hand. Write $v_0, v_1, v_2$ for the three states, with state 1 switched and $v_{\text{flag}} = 0$. The Bellman equations (Lesson 26) are

$$\begin{aligned} v_0 &= -1 + p\,v_1 + (1-p)\,v_0 \\ v_1 &= -1 + p\,v_0 + (1-p)\,v_2 \\ v_2 &= -1 + p \cdot 0 + (1-p)\,v_1 \end{aligned}$$

The first gives $v_0 = v_1 - 1/p$. Substituting both others into the second gives $v_1\,p(1-p) = -(3-p)$. So

$$J(p) = v_0 = -\frac{2\,(2-p)}{p\,(1-p)}$$

Setting $J'(p) = 0$ gives $p^2 - 4p + 2 = 0$, so the best policy picks right with $p = 2 - \sqrt2 \approx 0.59$ and earns $J \approx -11.66$. An ε-greedy agent with $\varepsilon = 0.1$ can only choose $p = 0.95$ or $p = 0.05$, worth $-44.2$ and $-82.1$.

Two reasons to learn the policy directly. The best policy may be stochastic, as here. And action probabilities change smoothly with $\boldsymbol\theta$, whereas an ε-greedy policy can flip completely when one estimate overtakes another.
